batch_name: Jesuit Alchemists: Schott and Lana Terzi
description: Two seventeenth-century Jesuit natural philosophers with significant alchemical interests: Gaspar Schott SJ (1608-1666), prolific author on natural magic, and Francesco Lana Terzi SJ (1631-1687), encyclopedist and experimenter. Both associated with Athanasius Kircher at the Collegio Romano. Primary source: Martha Baldwin, 'Alchemy and the Society of Jesus in the Seventeenth Century: Strange Bedfellows,' Ambix 40:2 (1993) pp.41-64.

persons.name: Gaspar Schott SJ
persons.bio_html:
Gaspar Schott (baptized 5 February 1608, Königshofen im Grabfeld, Bishopric of Würzburg – 22 May 1666, Würzburg) was a German Jesuit mathematician, natural philosopher, and prolific encyclopedist, known for his multi-volume works on natural magic, hydraulics, and experimental science. He is one of the principal intermediaries through whom the experimental and alchemical investigations of Athanasius Kircher were disseminated in mid-seventeenth-century Catholic Europe.

Schott entered the Society of Jesus and was forced to flee Germany during the Thirty Years' War when the political and confessional upheavals in his native Bishopric of Würzburg made life impossible for the Jesuit community. He spent nearly twenty years as a professor of mathematics and natural philosophy at the Jesuit college in Palermo, Sicily, before being transferred to Rome in 1652, where he lived at the Collegio Romano for three years and became a lifelong friend and devoted disciple of Kircher. He was initiated into Kircher's alchemical and natural-philosophical projects at the Collegio Romano, where he also met Francesco Lana Terzi. In 1655 he returned to Germany and settled at Würzburg, where he spent the remaining eleven years of his life in prolific publication.

Schott's published output was immense and encyclopedic. His major works include the Magia Universalis Naturae et Artis (4 vols., Würzburg, 1657–59), an exhaustive compendium of natural magic covering optics, acoustics, mathematics, and physics; the Mechanica Hydraulico-Pneumatica (Würzburg, 1657); the Thaumaturgus Physicus (1654), which devoted a chapter to pyrotechnic magic and the inextinguishable fires and fulminating gold of the alchemists; and the Cursus Mathematicus (1661). He also edited several of Kircher's works, including the Iter Exstaticum Coeleste (1660). Martha Baldwin, in 'Alchemy and the Society of Jesus in the Seventeenth Century' (Ambix 40:2, 1993), documents Schott's engagement with alchemy: he equivocated on the question of metallic transmutation, but was a firm believer in and experimenter on 'palingenesis' — the resurrection of plants from their calcined ashes — following recipes derived from Kircher and others. He also corresponded extensively with Leibniz, Otto von Guericke, and other leading natural philosophers of his day.

persons.name: Francesco Lana Terzi SJ
persons.bio_html:
Francesco Lana Terzi (1631, Brescia – 22 February 1687, Brescia) was an Italian Jesuit natural philosopher and encyclopedist, celebrated for his speculative designs for a lighter-than-air flying ship (an airship supported by evacuated copper spheres, described in his Prodromo of 1670) and for his ambitious attempt to compile an encyclopedic synthesis of natural philosophy and experiment in the Magisterium Artis et Naturae (2 vols., Brescia, 1684–86, with a third volume published posthumously).

Lana Terzi studied with Athanasius Kircher at the Collegio Romano in Rome from 1652 to 1654, where he was introduced to Kircher's laboratory-based natural philosophy and alchemical experiments. After teaching rhetoric and grammar at Jesuit gymnasia in Terni and Parma, he returned to his native Brescia in 1665, where he remained for the rest of his life pursuing physical, optical, and alchemical experiments. He taught mathematics at the University of Ferrara and the Jesuit college there before returning permanently to Brescia. He founded a local scientific society, the Accademia dei Filesotici, modelled on the Royal Society of London, and oversaw the publication of its journal, the Actae novae academiae philexeticorum naturae et artis, though both society and journal survived only briefly beyond his death in 1687. He corresponded with Leibniz, who published his letters in the Acta Eruditorum Lipsiae, and with the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society.

Martha Baldwin, in 'Alchemy and the Society of Jesus in the Seventeenth Century' (Ambix 40:2, 1993), documents Lana Terzi's sustained alchemical interests. He distinguished between alchemy and chemistry while accepting the three Hermetic principles of salt, sulphur, and mercury alongside the four Aristotelian elements. His Prodromo and Magisterium included recipes for chemical and medical preparations, and alchemical projects — including plant palingenesis experiments — engaged him throughout his career. His eclectic, Baconian approach to natural philosophy, combining Aristotelian, Hermetic, corpuscular, and magnetic concepts, typifies the intellectual syncretism of seventeenth-century Jesuit natural science.
